mcqs.question: What is the core idea behind loop tiling (blocking) as a cache optimization?
options: Replacing array indexing with pointer arithmetic for speed
Splitting a loop across multiple CPU cores to run in parallel
Reordering a loop so it always accesses memory in reverse
Processing data in small chunks that fit in a fast cache level, so each chunk is reused many times before eviction
mcqs.explanation: Tiling is specifically about sizing the working set of each pass to fit in cache, maximizing reuse before eviction. It's a single-threaded technique orthogonal to parallelism, isn't about reversing access order, and isn't about pointer-vs-index syntax (which typically compiles to the same code anyway).

mcqs.question: When does struct-of-arrays (SoA) layout outperform array-of-structs (AoS)?
options: When code scans a single field across many objects, since every byte of a fetched line is then useful data for that field
When code frequently reads/writes entire objects together, using all their fields at once
SoA is always faster than AoS regardless of access pattern
AoS and SoA always perform identically since they store the same data
mcqs.explanation: SoA wins specifically when the access pattern touches one field across many objects — every fetched cache line is then fully useful. If code instead processes whole objects at once, AoS keeps each object's fields together and is the better fit. Layout choice is very much access-pattern dependent, not universal.

mcqs.question: Two threads update logically independent counters that happen to sit on the same cache line, and performance is much worse than expected. What's the fix?
options: Add a mutex lock around each counter's update
Pad or separate the counters so each lands on its own cache line
Merge the two counters into a single shared variable
Switch both threads to use the same core
mcqs.explanation: This is false sharing — the coherence protocol invalidates the whole line on any write, even to an unrelated field on it. Locking adds overhead and doesn't fix the root cause; merging the variables would reintroduce real contention; the fix is purely a layout change, giving each variable its own cache line.

mcqs.question: A naive O(N^3) matrix multiply and a cache-blocked O(N^3) matrix multiply do the same number of arithmetic operations, yet the blocked version runs several times faster. What does this demonstrate?
options: That Big-O notation was calculated incorrectly for one of the versions
That blocked matrix multiply has a lower asymptotic complexity than naive multiply
That Big-O describes how cost scales with input size, but hides constant factors like cache behavior that dominate real wall-clock time
That the CPU's clock speed differs between the two runs
mcqs.explanation: Both are genuinely O(N^3) — the Big-O is identical and correctly calculated for both. The speed difference comes entirely from the hidden constant factor, driven here by cache hit rate, which asymptotic analysis by design doesn't capture. Clock speed is unrelated; it's the same CPU for both runs.

mcqs.question: A linked-list walk and an equivalent array scan touch the same number of elements, yet the array scan runs much faster. What's the key reason?
options: The array is always smaller in total bytes than the linked list
Linked-list nodes are stored in reverse order compared to arrays

An array's next address is predictable ahead of time, so the hardware prefetcher can stream it in; a linked list's next address is unknown until the current node is dereferenced, so it can't be prefetched
Arrays are always allocated on the stack, which is faster than heap memory
mcqs.explanation: The decisive factor is predictability: array elements sit at a fixed stride so the prefetcher can run ahead of the CPU, while a linked list's next address only becomes known after following the current pointer, so every step is effectively unpredictable and often a fresh miss. Total size, ordering, and stack-vs-heap placement aren't the mechanism.
